newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts see Skandia spinning off AFS unit.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Skandia spinning off AFS unit.

text.p: Analysts expect Swedish insurer Skandia to spin off and list its U.S. unit-linked division Assurance & Financial Services (AFS) within two to three years, even though Skandia says a stock-market listing is not yet on the agenda.

Skandia stock has soared in recent weeks as analysts preparing for news of some sort of spin-off upgrade the value of AFS. Speculation has been fuelled after U.S. insurer Hartford Financial listed its unit-linked Hartford Life division in May.
Skandia has said a listing is not on the agenda for AFS now.

"Skandia has done all the legal preparations to spin off AFS. But I don't think it could be a reality for two or three years," said Dresdner Kleinwort Benson analyst Nils Ringdahl in London on Wednesday. The house recently raised its target price for Skandia stock to 450 crowns by the beginning of 1999, citing strong growth in the AFS unit.
Since June 18 when the stock closed at 269 crowns it has kept breaking new territory, and made steady gains this week, closing up five crowns at 327.5 on Wednesday.
HSBC James Capel analyst Michael Broom said he expected Skandia to sell off AFS within two to five years.
"We would not be surprised to see a partial equity carve-out, or similar transaction, of AFS on a two to five year view," he told Reuters.
"(AFS chief executive Jan) Carendi has always said he could significantly increase its return on equity with more capital," Broom said.
"If, after such a transaction, Skandia for example ends up with a 70 percent stake in AFS, this could be worth more to Skandia than the 100 percent is worth today," he added.
"The return on capital could be grown significantly, (as a) virtue of the sales proceeds being reinvested in AFS," he said.
A partial listing of AFS, like Hartford Financial's recent move with its unit-linked Hartford Life division, would bring to light the unit's true value, analysts say.
One analyst, requesting anonymity, said such a move would be seen as shareholder-friendly.
Analysts also said Skandia could be trying to cover too many areas by holding on to AFS as a wholly-owned subsidiary.

"Sooner or later Skandia will be forced to do something about its ownership in AFS. Otherwise the old part of Skandia will have a secondary role and the group will be divided and less effective," one analyst said.
"At the same time I think they should take a firm grip on those areas which are not as profitable," the analyst added.

"In this context people should see the rumours of a merger with Trygg-Hansa for example. Both these companies are eager to make acquisitions and it's no secret that the question has been considered at the respective companies," he said.
Skandia announced last week AFS had more than $10 billion under management.

"1989 was American Skandia's first year in operation. Within a period of eight years, American Skandia has taken seventh place in the competitive U.S. life assurance market," chief executive Carendi said in a statement.
